title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

toc.title: 12.1 Photosynthetic pigments; photosystems I and II; the light reactions
12.2 Calvin cycle (C3), Hatch–Slack pathway (C4) and photorespiration; factors; bacterial photosynthesis

html:
The two great energy pathways share this chapter and its 3 of the 40 Botany questions. The paper's habits here are predictable: it asks where each step happens (thylakoid vs stroma, cytoplasm vs mitochondrion), the first products and CO₂ acceptors of the C3, C4 and CAM pathways, the book-keeping of ATP, NADH and CO₂ through the Calvin cycle and through glycolysis–Krebs–electron transport, and the respiratory quotient for different substrates. Learn the numbers in the tables below and the chapter converts directly into marks.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Pigments — chlorophyll a (primary, Mg centre) vs accessory b, carotenes, xanthophylls; absorption peaks in blue and red.
  • Light reactions — PS II = P680 (acts first), PS I = P700; Z-scheme water → NADP⁺; photolysis at the oxygen-evolving complex (Mn₄CaO₅) releases O₂ from water into the lumen; non-cyclic makes ATP + NADPH + O₂; cyclic (PS I only) makes ATP alone, topping the ratio to 3 ATP : 2 NADPH.
  • Calvin cycle (C3) — stroma; RuBP + CO₂ by RuBisCO → 2 × 3-PGA (first stable product); per CO₂: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH; per glucose: 18 ATP + 12 NADPH.
  • C4 (Hatch–Slack) — PEP carboxylase in mesophyll → oxaloacetate (4C) → malate → CO₂ released in bundle sheath (Kranz anatomy); spatial separation; 5 ATP per CO₂; maize, sugarcane.
  • Photorespiration — RuBisCO oxygenase; chloroplast–peroxisome–mitochondrion; loses 1 CO₂ per 2 oxygenations; worse when hot and stomata shut.
  • Factors — Blackman's law of limiting factors; light and CO₂ compensation points; airborne CO₂ is now about 0.043%, not 0.03%.
  • Bacterial photosynthesis — bacteriochlorophyll, H₂S as donor, no O₂ evolved.
  • Respiration — glycolysis (cytoplasm; net 2 ATP + 2 NADH → 2 pyruvate); link reaction (→ 2 acetyl-CoA + 2 CO₂ + 2 NADH); Krebs (matrix; per glucose 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ + 2 ATP + 4 CO₂); ETS on cristae, O₂ the terminal acceptor, chemiosmosis (Mitchell).
  • Totals and RQ — modern yield 30–32 ATP per glucose (classical 38); fermentation nets 2 ATP (all from glycolysis); RQ: carbohydrate 1.0, fat 0.7, protein 0.82, organic acids higher than 1; Pasteur effect.

12.1 Photosynthetic pigments; photosystems I and II; the light reactions

Photosynthesis reduces CO₂ to carbohydrate with water as the electron donor:

6 CO₂ + 12 H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ + 6 H₂O

Twelve waters stand on the left because all the released oxygen comes from water, not from CO₂ — predicted by van Niel from bacterial photosynthesis and proved with the heavy isotope ¹⁸O (Ruben and co-workers, 1941). The organelle is the chloroplast: pigments and electron carriers sit in the thylakoid membranes (stacked into grana, joined by stroma lamellae), protons are pumped into the lumen, and the carbon-fixing enzymes float in the stroma. Hold the rule: light reaction in the thylakoid, dark reaction in the stroma.

Of the pigments, only chlorophyll a — blue-green, with a magnesium atom at the centre of its porphyrin ring — can turn light into chemical energy: it is the primary pigment. Chlorophyll b, carotenes (orange) and xanthophylls (yellow) are accessory pigments: they harvest wavelengths chlorophyll a misses, pass the energy on, and (the carotenoids) protect against photo-oxidation. Chlorophyll absorbs strongly in the blue and red and reflects green — hence green leaves, and hence the action spectrum peaking in red and blue light.

Light is gathered by two antenna systems, each funnelling energy into a special pair of chlorophyll a molecules: photosystem II, reaction centre P680 (absorbance peak 680 nm, mostly in grana) and photosystem I, P700 (700 nm, mostly in stroma lamellae). Both are chlorophyll a; the numbers are wavelengths. Despite the names, PS II acts first — it was only discovered second.

In non-cyclic photophosphorylation electrons flow one way from water to NADP⁺ along the Z-scheme: light excites P680, which feeds electrons through pheophytin, the plastoquinone pool, the cytochrome b₆f complex and plastocyanin to PS I; light excites P700, which feeds them through ferredoxin to NADP⁺, forming NADPH. The hole left in P680 is so oxidising (+1.2 V) that the oxygen-evolving complex (Mn₄CaO₅, needing Cl⁻) on the lumen side of PS II can strip electrons from water — photolysis:

2 H₂O → O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻

Those protons, plus more pumped by cytochrome b₆f, build the lumen gradient whose discharge through ATP synthase makes ATP — chemiosmosis. Net products: ATP + NADPH + O₂.

In cyclic photophosphorylation PS I works alone: its electron returns from ferredoxin to the plastoquinone pool and round again, pumping protons but splitting no water — ATP only, no NADPH, no O₂. Its purpose is exact: the Calvin cycle needs ATP and NADPH in the ratio 3 : 2, linear flow supplies about 1.28, and cyclic flow makes up the shortfall.

Non-cyclic Cyclic
Photosystems PS II and PS I PS I only
Path open: water → NADP⁺ closed loop
Products ATP + NADPH + O₂ ATP only
Photolysis yes no
Main site grana stroma lamellae

The two ledgers the paper audits

Problem. How many ATP and NADPH does the Calvin cycle spend to make one glucose? What is the RQ of tripalmitin (C₅₁H₉₈O₆ + 72.5 O₂ → 51 CO₂ + 49 H₂O)? And the modern ATP total per glucose respired? Solution. Per CO₂ fixed the cycle spends 3 ATP + 2 NADPH; ×6 = 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose. RQ = 51 ÷ 72.5 ≈ 0.7 — the fat signature, hydrogen-rich fuel demanding extra oxygen. Respiration's ledger: 4 substrate-level ATP (2 glycolysis, 2 GTP) plus ~10 NADH × 2.5 and ~2 FADH₂ × 1.5 ≈ 25 + 3 = 28 oxidative → 30–32 ATP per glucose, against the 2 ATP of fermentation: oxygen is worth fifteen-fold.

12.2 Calvin cycle (C3), Hatch–Slack pathway (C4) and photorespiration; factors; bacterial photosynthesis

The Calvin cycle (Calvin, Benson, Bassham; Nobel 1961) runs in the stroma, light-independent but not nocturnal — it stops within minutes in the dark for want of ATP and NADPH.

  1. Carboxylation. The 5C acceptor ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP) takes CO₂, catalysed by RuBisCO (the most abundant protein on Earth, and a slow one). The 6C intermediate splits into two 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA, 3C) — the first stable product, hence "C3 plants".
  2. Reduction. Each 3-PGA is phosphorylated by 1 ATP and reduced by 1 NADPH to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P).
  3. Regeneration. Most G3P is reshuffled (costing 1 more ATP per CO₂) to rebuild RuBP; the surplus leaves to make sugars.

Book-keeping: per CO₂, 3 ATP + 2 NADPH; six turns give one glucose at 18 ATP + 12 NADPH, twelve G3P of which two exit and ten recycle.

Photorespiration. RuBisCO is also an oxygenase: in air it sometimes fixes O₂ instead of CO₂, yielding one 3-PGA and one useless 2-phosphoglycolate. Salvaging it tours three organelles — chloroplast → peroxisome → mitochondrion — burns ATP and releases one CO₂ for every two oxygenations, with no ATP gain. It worsens as temperature rises and as closed stomata let internal CO₂ fall.

C4 photosynthesis (Hatch and Slack, 1966) defeats photorespiration by concentrating CO₂ around RuBisCO, separating the two carboxylations in space. C4 leaves show Kranz anatomy: chloroplast-rich bundle-sheath cells wreathing the veins, ringed by mesophyll. In the mesophyll, PEP carboxylase (no oxygenase activity, high affinity) fixes bicarbonate onto PEP to give oxaloacetate (4C) — the first stable product — which is reduced to malate and shipped to the bundle sheath. There malate is decarboxylated, flooding RuBisCO with CO₂ at 10–20 times atmospheric levels, and the Calvin cycle runs almost free of oxygenation; pyruvate returns to regenerate PEP at a cost of two extra ATP equivalents per CO₂ (5 ATP + 2 NADPH total). Maize, sugarcane, sorghum and finger millet (kodo) are Nepal's C4 crops; rice and wheat are C3. CAM plants (pineapple, Aloe vera, Opuntia) achieve the same separation in time: stomata open at night, PEP carboxylase stores malic acid in the vacuole, and by day, behind closed stomata, the acid is decarboxylated for the Calvin cycle.

C3 C4 CAM
First stable product 3-PGA (3C) oxaloacetate (4C) oxaloacetate (4C)
First CO₂ acceptor/enzyme RuBP / RuBisCO PEP / PEP carboxylase PEP / PEP carboxylase
Separation none spatial (Kranz) temporal (night/day)

ATP per CO₂ 3 5 5–6
Stomata open day day night

Bacterial photosynthesis (purple and green sulphur bacteria) uses bacteriochlorophyll, one photosystem, and donors such as H₂S instead of water — so it deposits sulphur and evolves no oxygen (anoxygenic). Comparing it with plant photosynthesis is what led van Niel to locate the oxygen's source in water.

Factors. Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905): the rate is set by whichever factor is nearest its minimum. The light compensation point is where photosynthesis exactly balances respiration (no net gas exchange); the CO₂ compensation point is the equivalent CO₂ level (40–100 ppm in C3, only 3–10 in C4). CO₂ in air is now about 427 ppm (0.043%) and is usually the field's limiting factor; red and blue light are most effective; temperature governs through enzyme kinetics (rate roughly doubling per 10 °C to an optimum, then crashing); water shortage acts by closing stomata.

12.3 Aerobic and anaerobic respiration: glycolysis, oxidative decarboxylation, Krebs cycle, electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation; factors

Respiration releases the energy of food in controlled packets, trapping much of it in ATP:

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + energy (ΔG ≈ −2870 kJ mol⁻¹)

1. Glycolysis (Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas pathway) runs in the cytoplasm of every cell, with or without oxygen. Glucose is phosphorylated twice — 2 ATP invested, at hexokinase and at the rate-limiting phosphofructokinase — then split into two triose phosphates, each oxidised (making NADH) and each yielding 2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. Net: 2 ATP + 2 NADH + 2 pyruvate (3C) per glucose. No CO₂ yet.

2. Link reaction (oxidative decarboxylation). In the mitochondrial matrix the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts each pyruvate (3C) to acetyl-CoA (2C) + CO₂ + NADH: per glucose, 2 CO₂ + 2 NADH. It is irreversible, which is why fat cannot be turned back into sugar by reversing it.

3. Krebs cycle (citric acid/TCA cycle, Krebs 1937), also in the matrix. Acetyl-CoA (2C) joins oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C) → α-ketoglutarate (5C) → succinyl-CoA (4C) → succinate → fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate again. Per turn: 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 ATP + 2 CO₂; per glucose (two turns): 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ + 2 ATP + 4 CO₂. Note that all six glucose carbons have now left as CO₂ and no O₂ has been used.

4. Electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation. The 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂ are cashed at the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae): Complex I → ubiquinone → Complex III → cytochrome c → Complex IV → oxygen, the terminal electron acceptor, which with protons forms water. FADH₂ enters at Complex II, bypassing I — which is why it yields less. Complexes I, III and IV pump protons (10 H⁺ per NADH, 6 per FADH₂), and their return through ATP synthase drives ATP formation — Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis (Nobel 1978). With about 4 H⁺ spent per ATP, an NADH is worth 2.5 ATP and an FADH₂ 1.5, giving the modern total of 30–32 ATP per glucose (the shuttle used by the two cytoplasmic NADH decides between 30 and 32). The classical figure of 38 ATP assumed 3 per NADH and 2 per FADH₂; if a question specifies those ratios, use them.

Anaerobic respiration (fermentation). Without oxygen the chain stalls and NADH piles up; fermentation exists to regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue. Alcoholic fermentation (yeast, flooded roots): pyruvate → acetaldehyde (pyruvate decarboxylase) → ethanol + CO₂. Lactic acid fermentation (muscle, Lactobacillus): pyruvate → lactate, no CO₂. Fermentation itself makes zero ATP — the whole anaerobic yield is glycolysis's 2 ATP, about 8% of the aerobic prize, which is why switching on oxygen sharply cuts glucose consumption (the Pasteur effect).

Respiratory quotient. RQ = CO₂ evolved ÷ O₂ consumed (Ganong's respirometer), and it betrays the substrate: carbohydrates 1.0, fats ≈ 0.7 (oxygen-poor, so they gulp external O₂), proteins ≈ 0.82, organic acids higher than 1 (malic 1.33, oxalic 4.0 — already oxygen-rich), fermenting tissue undefined (no O₂ taken up).

Worked example — costs and quotients

Problem. (a) How many ATP and NADPH does the Calvin cycle spend to export one net G3P? (b) Germinating seeds in a respirometer evolve 45 cm³ of CO₂ while taking up 50 cm³ of O₂. Find the RQ and comment.

Solution. (a) A net G3P contains 3 carbons, so three turns fix 3 CO₂. At 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂:

3 \times 3 = 9\ \text{ATP}, \qquad 3 \times 2 = 6\ \text{NADPH}

(One glucose, two G3P, doubles this to 18 ATP + 12 NADPH.)

(b)

\text{RQ} = \frac{45}{50} = 0.9

Below 1 but above the fat value of 0.7: the seeds are respiring a mixture — largely fat or protein with some carbohydrate — as oily seeds (mustard, castor) do while converting their stores.

Factors affecting respiration. Oxygen: below a few percent the rate falls and fermentation takes over. Temperature: rate roughly doubles per 10 °C (Q₁₀ ≈ 2) up to about 35–40 °C, then enzyme damage cuts it. Water: dry seeds respire almost imperceptibly (why grain stores safely), and imbibition switches respiration on. CO₂: high concentrations depress respiration — exploited in controlled-atmosphere fruit storage. Light acts only indirectly, through temperature and photosynthate supply.

Worked example — the ATP account for one glucose (modern values)

Count carefully, stage by stage, per glucose molecule:

  • Glycolysis (cytoplasm): 4 ATP made by substrate-level phosphorylation, 2 spent → net 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH in the cytoplasm (worth about 1.5–2.5 ATP each depending on the shuttle used).
  • Oxidative decarboxylation (per glucose: two pyruvates) → 2 mitochondrial NADH.
  • Krebs cycle (two turns) → 2 ATP (GTP) directly, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂.
  • Electron transport at roughly 2.5 ATP per mitochondrial NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂ gives a grand total of about 30–32 ATP — the modern figure. (Older books quote 36–38 using 3 and 2 ATP per NADH/FADH₂; if an MCQ lists 38 as an option, the paper is using the traditional accounting.)

The robust facts are the net numbers per stage — learn those, and either total can be reconstructed.

Trap — O₂ comes from water, not from CO₂

Isotope experiments settled it: the oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from splitting water (photolysis) at photosystem II, not from carbon dioxide. Pairs with a second swap: cyclic photophosphorylation makes ATP only (PS I alone, no NADPH, no O₂), while non-cyclic flow (PS II + PS I) makes ATP + NADPH + O₂.

Common mistake

Four pairs the paper swaps: the evolved O₂ comes from water, not CO₂ (¹⁸O labelling settled it); PSII acts first in the chain though named second — numbering follows discovery, electrons follow energy; the Calvin cycle sits in the stroma, not on the thylakoid, and needs light only via ATP and NADPH; and photorespiration consumes, it does not produce — CO₂ out, ATP spent, no sugar, which is exactly why C₄ exists.

Formula and fact sheet

  • Sites: light reactions thylakoid (grana/lamellae), O₂ from water (¹⁸O proof); Calvin stroma; glycolysis cytoplasm; link + Krebs matrix; ETS cristae.
  • Photosystems: PS II P680 acts first, PS I P700; order H₂O → PS II → PQ → cyt b₆f → plastocyanin → PS I → ferredoxin → NADP⁺.
  • Products: non-cyclic ATP + NADPH + O₂; cyclic ATP only (ratio repair to 3 : 2).
  • Calvin: RuBP acceptor, RuBisCO, first product 3-PGA; 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂; 18 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose.
  • C4: PEP/PEP carboxylase → OAA → malate → bundle sheath (Kranz); 5 ATP per CO₂; compensation 3–10 ppm. CAM: same chemistry by night, stomata shut by day.
  • Photorespiration: RuBisCO oxygenase; chloroplast–peroxisome–mitochondrion; 1 CO₂ lost per 2 oxygenations; hot + closed stomata worsens it.
  • Bacterial photosynthesis: bacteriochlorophyll, H₂S donor, no O₂.
  • Respiration tallies per glucose: glycolysis net 2 ATP + 2 NADH; link 2 NADH + 2 CO₂; Krebs 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ + 2 ATP + 4 CO₂; carriers total 10 NADH + 2 FADH₂.
  • Yields: NADH ≈ 2.5 ATP, FADH₂ ≈ 1.5 → 30–32 per glucose (classical 3/2 gives 38); fermentation 2 (glycolysis only, regenerates NAD⁺).
  • RQ: glucose 1.0, fat 0.7, protein 0.82, malic acid 1.33, oxalic 4.0; measured by Ganong's respirometer.
  • People: van Niel and Ruben (O₂ from water), Calvin (cycle), Hatch and Slack (C4), Krebs (cycle), Mitchell (chemiosmosis), Blackman (limiting factors).

Chapter summary

  • Chlorophyll a (Mg-centred) alone converts light energy; accessory pigments widen the catch and protect the reaction centres P680 (PS II, acting first) and P700 (PS I).
  • The Z-scheme drags electrons from water (photolysis at the Mn₄CaO₅ complex, O₂ and protons into the lumen) to NADP⁺, minting ATP chemiosmotically on the way; cyclic flow around PS I adds ATP only, balancing the 3 : 2 budget.
  • The stromal Calvin cycle carboxylates RuBP via RuBisCO into 3-PGA and, at 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂, builds glucose for 18 ATP + 12 NADPH.
  • Photorespiration — RuBisCO fixing O₂ — wastes carbon through a three-organelle salvage loop; C4 plants suppress it spatially (Kranz anatomy, PEP carboxylase pump, 5 ATP per CO₂) and CAM plants temporally.
  • Blackman's limiting-factor law and the two compensation points govern how light, CO₂ (now 0.043%), temperature and water set the photosynthetic rate; bacteria photosynthesise with H₂S and release no O₂.
  • Glycolysis (cytoplasm) nets 2 ATP + 2 NADH; the link reaction and Krebs cycle (matrix) strip the six carbons out as CO₂, loading 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂ in all.
  • The cristae electron-transport chain, ending at oxygen, converts those carriers into most of the modern 30–32 ATP per glucose (38 classically).
  • Without oxygen, fermentation merely regenerates NAD⁺ for glycolysis's 2 ATP (Pasteur effect), and the RQ — 1.0, 0.7, 0.82, above 1 — reports the substrate being burned.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (c) — Chlorophyll a forms the reaction centres; the others only gather light and hand the energy over.

2. (b) — Mg²⁺ sits in the porphyrin ring; iron belongs to haem and cytochromes.

3. (a) — P680 and P700 name absorption maxima in nm; both centres are chlorophyll a.

4. (a) — Proved with ¹⁸O-labelled water by Ruben and co-workers (1941).

5. (c) — The Mn₄CaO₅ complex faces the lumen of PS II, so photolysis protons feed the ATP gradient.

6. (a) — Linear flow from water to NADP⁺ yields both currencies and oxygen.

7. (d) — Electrons cycle around PS I only: ATP without NADPH or O₂.

8. (b) — Ferredoxin–NADP⁺ reductase completes the Z-scheme by making NADPH.

9. (a) — The 6C addition product splits instantly into two 3-PGA — the "3" of C3.

10. (c) — The 5C RuBP is regenerated each turn to accept the next CO₂.

11. (d) — RuBisCO, the Earth's most abundant protein, carboxylates (and, unluckily, oxygenates) RuBP.

12. (b) — PEP carboxylase makes the 4C oxaloacetate first; malate is its reduced transport form.

13. (c) — The wreath of bundle-sheath cells around the veins houses the C4 Calvin cycle.

14. (d) — Phosphoglycolate salvage runs chloroplast → peroxisome → mitochondrion, leaking CO₂.

15. (a) — Blackman (1905): the scarcest factor sets the rate.

16. (d) — Anoxygenic photosynthesis with bacteriochlorophyll; sulphur is deposited instead of O₂ released.

17. (b) — Glycolysis is universal and cytoplasmic; only later stages enter the mitochondrion.

18. (c) — Four ATP made by substrate-level phosphorylation minus two invested = net 2.

19. (c) — Oxidative decarboxylation: 3C pyruvate → 2C acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH.

20. (d) — The matrix holds the cycle; the cristae hold the electron transport chain.

21. (b) — Plus 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP and 2 CO₂ per turn.

22. (b) — Oxygen accepts the electrons and protons to form water; without it the chain stalls.

23. (c) — Peter Mitchell, Nobel Prize 1978; the same mechanism makes ATP in chloroplasts.

24. (d) — Glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 CO₂; lactic fermentation, by contrast, releases no CO₂.

25. (a) — Six CO₂ out for six O₂ in: RQ = 1.0 for carbohydrates.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (a) — PS I was characterised first, though in the chain PS II feeds it.

2. (a) — Linear flow gives an ATP : NADPH ratio near 1.28; cyclic flow tops it up to the required 1.5.

3. (d) — No photon is used directly, but the substrates ATP and NADPH run out quickly in the dark.

4. (d) — The PEP-carboxylase pump swamps the oxygenase reaction by sheer CO₂ pressure.

5. (b) — Night air is cool and humid; CO₂ is banked as malic acid and spent behind closed stomata by day.

6. (b) — Trapped O₂ from photolysis plus dwindling CO₂ tips RuBisCO towards oxygenation.

7. (d) — CO₂ taken up in photosynthesis equals CO₂ released in respiration.

8. (c) — Reducing pyruvate re-oxidises NADH; the ATP all comes from glycolysis itself.
